Elastic N.V. recently reported fiscal first-quarter 2027 results, with revenue rising to US$478.11 million and net loss narrowing to US$16.73 million, while also issuing guidance that points to continued revenue growth through fiscal 2027.

Alongside the earnings beat and raised outlook, Elastic highlighted growing enterprise adoption of its AI-powered search and cloud platform, and disclosed that non-executive director Caryn Marooney will step down after her term ends in October 2026.

Against this backdrop of stronger-than-expected results and higher full-year guidance, we'll now examine how Elastic's AI-driven momentum influences its investment narrative.

Elastic Investment Narrative Recap

To own Elastic, you really need to believe its AI‑powered search, security, and observability platform can stay differentiated even as competition and pricing pressure build. Right now, the key near term catalyst is execution on its AI and cloud adoption story, and the biggest risk is that rising investment needs or weaker demand compress margins. The latest earnings beat and raised guidance support the catalyst, while Caryn Marooney's planned board exit does not materially change that risk profile.

The most relevant recent development here is Elastic's updated guidance, calling for Q2 FY2027 revenue of US$486–487 million and full year FY2027 revenue of US$1.998–2.010 billion. That outlook sits alongside management's emphasis on AI‑driven customer adoption, reinforcing the idea that execution on AI monetization and cloud consumption remains central to the story and to whether Elastic can offset competitive and cost pressures over the next few quarters.

VOOG's recent lead is period-specific, and over five years the gap narrows to 88% vs 80%, making it a bet on AI concentration continuing to pay.

Investors who pick growth ETFs based solely on expense ratio are optimizing the least important variable in 2026. Vanguard Growth ETF (NYSEARCA:VUG) charges an ultra-low 0.03%, while Vanguard S&P 500 Growth ETF (NYSEARCA:VOOG) costs 0.07%, yet VOOG has been the better performer year to date and over the trailing 12 months.

jamesteohart

Year to date, VOOG has returned roughly 14%, compared with about 10% for VUG, a gap wider than four basis points of fees could explain. Over the trailing twelve months, VOOG is up about 22%, compared with roughly 16% for VUG. Both funds hold roughly 150 mega-cap growth names, so the divergence stems from how the underlying indexes weight the shared holdings.

Same Universe, Different Rulebooks

VUG tracks the Morningstar US Large Cap Growth Index while VOOG follows the S&P 500 Growth Index, drawing only from S&P 500 constituents classified as growth. The overlap in top holdings is heavy, but individual weights differ meaningfully.

NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) accounts for 13.3% of VUG and nearly 14.3% of VOOG, while Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) accounts for 12.3% of VUG and only 6.4% of VOOG. Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) shows up at 5.9% in VOOG versus 4.4% in VUG, and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) is close to a tie at 9.1% in VUG and 9.3% in VOOG. Those single-digit weighting gaps compound across the largest positions in both portfolios.

title: Okta (OKTA) Grew Remaining Performance Obligations 17% While Revenue Rose 11%. Is the Platform Reaccelerating?
detail:
Okta (OKTA) Grew Remaining Performance Obligations 17% While Revenue Rose 11%. Is the Platform Reaccelerating?
Jeff Lewis
Fri, August 28, 2026 at 11:17 PM EDT 4 min read

Okta, Inc. (NASDAQ:OKTA) reported fiscal second-quarter 2027 results that strengthened the case for a bookings recovery. Revenue rose 11% year over year to $805 million, while company-defined non-GAAP diluted earnings increased 15% to $1.05 per share. Consensus estimates called for revenue of $793 million and adjusted earnings of $0.97 per share.

The more important signal was in contracted business. Remaining performance obligations, or subscription backlog, increased 17% to $4.858 billion, outpacing recognized revenue growth by six percentage points. Current RPO, which Okta, Inc. (NASDAQ:OKTA) expects to recognize over the next 12 months, grew 14% to $2.585 billion.

Both measures accelerated from the first quarter, when RPO and cRPO grew 16% and 12%, respectively. The contracted subscription backlog of Okta, Inc. (NASDAQ:OKTA) is therefore growing faster than recognized revenue, although RPO can also move with contract duration and deal timing. One quarter of stronger backlog growth is encouraging, but it does not establish a durable trend by itself.

Why Okta, Inc. (OKTA) Crashed Last Week
Bull Case

There are signs that the broader platform strategy is contributing. New products represented approximately 30% of second-quarter bookings, up from roughly 25% in the first quarter, and Okta Identity Governance remained the largest contributor. Management said contracts containing at least one new product carried an average annual contract value uplift of about 40%. Customers with at least $1 million in annual contract value also grew 22% to 605 and represented more than $1 billion in aggregate ACV. That supports the case that Okta, Inc. (NASDAQ:OKTA) is selling more than basic authentication, although the new-product mix merely returned to the 30% level reported in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026.

AI agents could widen that opportunity. As companies deploy software agents that act across applications and data, those agents require identities, permissions and governance. Okta, Inc. (NASDAQ:OKTA) has expanded its AI-agent offering with capabilities covering sign-on, agent-to-agent connections and access certification. Management disclosed dozens of AI-agent deals, including several transactions worth more than $1 million. Those contracts demonstrate early customer demand, although management said the category remained too small to appear separately in reported results. For now, AI is a credible market-expansion argument rather than a separately measurable growth engine.

The recovery also reached reported profitability. GAAP operating income rose to $107 million from $41 million, lifting the GAAP operating margin to 13% from 6%. Company-defined non-GAAP operating margin held at 28%. Free cash flow increased to $227 million from $162 million, while its margin expanded to 28% from 22%. Okta, Inc. (NASDAQ:OKTA) defines free cash flow as operating cash flow minus purchases of property and equipment, net of proceeds, and capitalized software.

title: Has Microsoft Stock Run Ahead Of Its AI Payoff?
detail:
Has Microsoft Stock Run Ahead Of Its AI Payoff?
Trefis Team

MSFT
GOOG
AMZN
AAPL
ORCL
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image by Pexels from Pixabay

The software giant's stock has a powerful business engine behind its long-term trend, but a rapid run-up back toward all-time highs forces investors to ask if the price of admission is still worth paying.

Microsoft (MSFT) has built one of the most durable cash-generation engines in enterprise technology, but its stock currently trades about 6% below its 52-week high. For any investor sizing up the company's dominant push into artificial intelligence, the central question is clear: is this a consolidation pause before another leg higher, or has the current price already captured the payoff? While the stock's broader trend strength ranks near the middle of US-listed stocks above $1B, the recent rally to within 6% of its 52-week high brings the core tension into focus: does the fundamental engine justify the elevated valuation?

The core investment case rests on this underlying operational momentum rather than technical strength, raising the question of whether the current price offers sufficient upside for new buyers.

Is This a Genuine Business Surge?

The numbers behind Microsoft's run are strong. The company's operating margin over the last twelve months is a huge 47%, far outpacing the S&P 500 median of 18.5%. This isn't a one-time event; its three-year average is similarly high. Revenue growth tells the same story, at 17.8% over the past year, more than double the 8.3% median for the index.

This financial power comes directly from its strategic execution in AI and cloud computing. In its most recent quarter, revenue from Azure and other cloud services grew 43%, a clear sign that demand for its AI services is intense. Management confirmed that "Customer demand continues to exceed available capacity." The adoption of its AI tools is also rapid, with the company reporting it now has "over 30 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats."

What Does a Share of This Engine Cost?

The market is well aware of this operational strength, and it charges a premium. Microsoft trades at a price-to-earnings multiple of 28.0, compared to an S&P 500 median of 23.3. That premium exists even after a stretch of relative underperformance: over the trailing twelve months, Microsoft has been largely flat, trailing the S&P 500's +21% return. The stock also trades about 6% below its two-year high of $537.65, reinforcing that buyers today are not chasing a fresh peak.

The primary risk centers on the sheer scale of capital expenditure required to sustain this AI buildout. Some analysts are asking if soaring capital expenditures could put the stock's valuation at risk. The concern is that the company is building for a level of demand that might not materialize, or that rising component costs could squeeze profitability. This risk is compounded by declines in legacy businesses. Management expects revenue from its Windows OEM and Devices segment to "decline in the high teens for the fiscal year," and Xbox revenue recently decreased 10%. For investors who prefer broader exposure to the technology sector without concentrating on a single company's execution risk, a technology ETF like VGT might be an alternative.

title: Why ZM Stock Prints So Much Cash Right Now
detail:
Why ZM Stock Prints So Much Cash Right Now
Trefis Team

MSFT
CRM
CSCO
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by Luca Sammarco on Pexels

The video-call giant is generating far more cash than the average company, yet the market is treating it like a business in decline. Here's the offer on the table.

The market is offering a cash machine at a discount, which raises the central question for any investor: is this a high-yield bargain, or is the market correctly pricing in a future breakdown?

The cash flow is built on a profitable, expanding platform. Zoom (ZM)'s ability to generate cash is not a recent fluke. The company has produced positive free cash flow in every twelve-month period for the last three years, totaling $1.93 billion in the most recent stretch. This is the output of a highly profitable operation, with a trailing operating margin of 24%, well above the 18.5% S&P 500 median. The balance sheet is also clean, with net cash of about $7.2 billion, meaning the high yield isn't an illusion created by debt. The machine behind these numbers is Zoom's strategic shift from a single-product application to an integrated communications platform.

While revenue growth of 5.0% over the last year trails the 8.3% median for large companies, management is focused on selling a broader "AI-first system of action." This includes products like Zoom Phone and Zoom Contact Center, which are driving larger, multi-year deals with corporate clients. The market is pricing a gap between new wins and existing customer spend. The offer exists because the market sees a contradiction in Zoom's story. On one hand, the push into the enterprise is showing clear results. Enterprise revenue recently grew 7.8%, its strongest rate in three years. The company's remaining performance obligations, which represent future contracted revenue, jumped 14% to $4.5 billion, signaling success in landing bigger commitments.

But there is a catch. The company's trailing 12-month net dollar expansion rate for enterprise customers was 99%. In simple terms, for every dollar Zoom received from its existing enterprise clients a year ago, it now gets 99 cents. Upsells and cross-sells are being slightly offset by churn and downgrades. This creates a difficult situation where growth depends heavily on winning new customers, because the current base isn't expanding its spend. Compounding this, management's latest outlook assumes "flat online growth," putting the full weight of the company's future on that enterprise segment. The entire offer hinges on turning new platform deals into net expansion. The debate over Zoom's value boils down to this tension. The company is a cash-rich, highly profitable business that is successfully winning larger deals with new enterprise customers. Yet it has not yet proven it can consistently expand spending within its existing customer base.
